title: Notes of Ministry - 19 - June 1974

paragraphs.text: I have been thinking of how we need to have the complete idea of the body before us and, in principle, to work it out locally. The mystery relates to the Head in heaven and the body upon earth. There is one body, of which each one who has the Spirit is a member, but we have the privilege, as we have brethren with whom to work things out, to provide an expression of the body locally. The mystery involves that the Head is in heaven and the body here, but it is not that the expression of the body here is a headless body. Paul would adjust any such thought as that by saying, “We have the mind of Christ” (1 Corinthians 2: 16), indicating that the complete idea of the body can be worked out in every locality. Reference is made here to the head; the head should not say to the feet, “I have not need of you”. Therefore, we are not speaking of a headless body. Whilst Christ is the Head in heaven, the blessed Spirit brings the value of His headship to be worked out in persons here.

In the face of the tremendous changes that have taken place amongst us in recent years we need to think of the need for reconstruction of the local representation of the body. When we met together with large numbers we were often reminded that we were only a fraction of those who form the body in any locality. How much more so when numbers have been reduced so severely. We feel for our brethren in places where there are only two or three brothers, but even in such cases it is the mind of God that there should be an expression of the body locally.

The body is an interesting consideration, because when man was formed out of the dust of the ground, divine skill and wisdom entered into the formation of his body. Doctors and scientists are continually finding something new in the intricacies of the mystery of the human body—it is God’s handiwork. But this is to be seen representatively, spiritually, in our localities.

Man said of the woman, “Bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh”, Genesis 2: 23. The bones give the basis for man being upright; there is what is structural; being upright requires balance. Balance is one of the greatest needs amongst us. The seat of balance is the inner ear, indicating to us so strikingly how balance and regulation come by way of the word of God.

The necessity for meetings like this, therefore, would impress itself upon us. If we are to be preserved in balance we must be attentive to God’s word. We stand on the principle of balance, but we do more than stand on the principle of balance; we have two ears, which indicates the need for balanced hearing. With two ears we have the facility to detect quickly the source from which a voice, or sound, comes. It is a matter of focus. Whilst hearing is one thought, mutuality of hearing in the local company is essential if we are to detect, corporately, the source from which the sound emanates. These are days when this mutual function of hearing is most necessary because there are many voices abroad. Much is being said; the enemy is using all kinds of speaking to throw the dear brethren off balance. To hear rightly we should be often together, speaking one to another. It is thus that we will be held, mutually, in balance.

The body has two eyes. To see things in proper perspective requires focus. The third dimension in our seeing is arrived at through mutual and focused sight, thus providing a balanced view of things. We want to be preserved from narrowness or limitation; we want to have keen sight like the eagle, but it is a mutual matter. Let us share together what we see.

Mr. Taylor Sen. said very wisely that if we get an impression, get it into the assembly as soon as possible so that it will be put into proper balance and kept within the banks of the river; thus the truth will not be distorted.

The body has one mouth—which does not mean that only one brother does the speaking, but rather that there is unity. Paul told the Corinthians that the Son of God was preached by himself and Silvanus and Timotheus (2 Corinthians 1: 19); three servants, but one mouth. Paul says, “that ye may with one accord, with one mouth, glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ,” Romans 15: 6. It is a wonderful thing when all the brethren are saying the same thing. So Paul exhorts the Corinthians to think the same thing and to say the same thing. It does not mean that there is not variety, but it is all one piece. The preaching of Timotheus would be different from the preaching of Paul, but he was preaching the Son of God. It was one mouth.

The body has two hands. There is what is mutual, and what is unified. The arms would represent a wider function than the hands, relating more to power; the hands relate more to detail. Holy hands are to be lifted in prayer. We find that power comes in through the lifting up of holy hands. We often come before God in prayer. What is the result of our prayers? Do we have power in prayer? Power in prayer will result from the right use of our hands in ordinary matters as well as in relation to the things of God.

We could go on and delineate in detail, because not only is there the bony structure, but there is also the flesh, which suggests the working of things organically. This could be spoken of for profit. We are to have concern as to the right functioning of the organs, some of which are automatic, but all should contribute to the life and activity in the locality. But my concern at the moment is that through reduction of numbers there should be no loss of body function.

Previously I may have had some little service to fill out, but now I may find that there are others things I must engage in to fill out body function—otherwise there will be a lack in the locality. If we all feel like that it may be possible so to develop local body feelings and function that there is a true representation of the body in our localities. It will mean that we will have to take on additional responsibilities and exercises to make up for what has been lost.

The Lord said of the woman of Luke 7, “She from the time I came in has not ceased kissing my feet”. She was kissing His feet because of love for Him, but that love felt what Simon did not do, and she was filling the need that was there through the neglect of Simon. So, as we find our numbers reduced, there is more for us to do, but let us be contributors to an increased yield to the Lord and in maintaining a brighter testimony in our localities. We can understand what an exercise this must be to those in places where there are very few brethren—just two or three, but, at the same time, the Spirit of God will help because the body is one, and any representation of it should be complete.

In these things, dear brethren, we need the Spirit’s help, not only to be able to apprehend what there should be in the locality testimonially and functionally, but that these things are held in the heart of each of the saints in a fuller way on account of the fewness of numbers.
Thus we will be concerned that there may be no part missing, and no lack.

articles.title: A SECOND COMMITTAL
articles.author: G. D. Pfingst
articles.place: Word at meeting for ministry, Brooklyn, N.Y.

paragraphs.text: I was impressed by our brother mentioning in his prayer the solemnity of occasions such as this. I believe that the very solemn occasion of which we have read has been referred to as the second covenant that God made with His people of old. We all have been under responsibility; we cannot say that we were under covenant in the same sense as God’s earthly people, but we have made vows in putting our hands to the Supper, involving faithfulness to the Lord. Much has come in to divert us, so that possibly a second committal is needed.

We do well to remind ourselves of the solemnity of the things to which we have committed ourselves. It is the day of grace and we are not under law, nor do we seek to put anyone else under law. We know the One who has kept the law and made it honourable; the One who took our place on Calvary’s cross and bore our sins in His body on the tree; things have been fulfilled in Him, but nevertheless we are responsible to be faithful.

What a wonderful day of grace it is! What could not be kept by man under law can be kept by those who now walk according to Spirit. There is the side of responsibility in maintaining the testimony, but there is the power, in the Spirit, to fulfil that responsibility. But we may need to enter into a second committal to be more faithful than we have been in the past. One would seek to encourage us in that way. I know how I have failed in the past; many times I was careless, but God would just pull us up, as it were, and have us take stock as to where we stand, and how much we recognise the authority we are under.

We are told that when Mr. Darby came out of the organised church he went through deep exercise and pressure, feeling the responsibility of being obedient to the authority of God’s word. And we have the authority of God’s word. Moses, in the verses we have read, represents that authority; he stands up with the people. There is the authority of God’s word today. If we maintain fresh links with the Lord and recognise the authority of God’s word, what blessing there is for us: His word will lead us according to 2 Timothy 2, which is the path for us at the present time. The church, as such, has lost its authority—we are in a day of breakdown, but the authoritative side continues in the acceptance of the word of God. We must not disregard it. 2 Timothy 2 supposes that there will always be those that call on the Lord out of a pure heart, and we can speak of those that are “here with us this day”. It is a matter of being with the Lord in things, of course, but we can thank God that there are those with whom we can work out the truth. The Lord would not have us walk alone.

How can we encourage persons to be with us? We do not want to make much of ourselves; we do not assume any position; we do not want to be presumptuous in any way, but brethren who have part in this second committal should be aware of their responsibility to support the testimony. We do not want to force any one; we are not establishing attendance officers, but we do want to see our brethren at the meetings. Seeing the brethren should stimulate mutual encouragement. Moses spoke of “him that standeth here with us this day”. With such, the covenant is to be made so that we shall not be turned aside to other things.

There is a danger of that at the present time. The enemy is using the world and its allurements to attract the Lord’s people. It has been said that he is not too much concerned about those who already are in the world, because he has such under his influence. But the world and its attractions are presented in their various phases to attract persons at every stage of spiritual life. We hardly realise the tremendous power the enemy wields at the present time, seeking to get into every area of our responsible history to divert and overwhelm us. But let us not be overwhelmed. These things are written so that we might freshly commit ourselves to the testimony. We need not be overwhelmed in any way, but rather be balanced as we adhere to this wonderful covenant that is made here this day with all the people.

This is the point I desire to make, dear brethren. I cannot say much about these things, for I feel how shallow I am, but the Scripture has its own weight and authority, and we can get help just in reading it. Let us therefore be concerned about this reference to a second committal and, with those that stand here this day devote ourselves in a fresh way to the support of the testimony. It is a time to stand—“Having accomplished all things, to stand”, Ephesians 6: 13. The goal and the prize of the calling on high of God in Christ Jesus are just before us. Let us be ready and watching, that we be not ashamed at His coming. One would just seek to encourage each one here so that, in spite of hardships, in spite of pressures, in spite of all that has come upon us, we may stand—“stand before Jehovah”.

Then Moses referred to “him that is not here with us this day.” To apply this practically, I would ask, Are there any that are not here with us this day? We would like to see them. Our meetings have been arranged so that most of our brethren in the city can attend without being overburdened or oppressed; therefore, we would like to see them with us “this day”. But note that the covenant was made with him that was not present, too. So that though persons may not be here with us on this occasion, the covenant is made with them; they must not excuse themselves.

I would like to encourage every one to be with the saints in current matters. Being with the Lord is essential; you must have your personal links with the Lord or you will founder, but you also need active links with the brethren—with those who call upon the Lord out of a pure heart. It is wonderful that there can be a second committal. If we have

drifted, or in any way have gotten into byways, there is this second opportunity to make fresh committals to be with the brethren in support of current exercises and to contribute to assembly life, and be preserved from what is defiling and damaging in the world. Let us, therefore, stand firmly with the saints, for His name’s sake.

“At that time, Jesus answering said, I praise thee, Father, Lord of the heaven and of the earth, that thou hast hid these things from the wise and prudent, and hast revealed them to babes. Yea, Father, for thus has it been well-pleasing in thy sight”, Matthew 11: 25.

Think of being the subject of conversation between divine Persons! Is it not attractive that we may put ourselves in there? Has heaven ceased to talk in that way? No indeed! The greatest exercise is to grasp what is current in heaven now. The gospels give us an inkling. There is continual joy there. The theme is largely the saints, and the joy and conversation in relation to them goes on.
J. Taylor, N.S. Vol. 41, p. 77

I read these scriptures, dear brethren, to call attention to this expression which is in each of them, “Fear not”. I think the first may be connected with the fear of God. The second we might link with the fear of self, and the third with the fear of circumstances; but the message in each case was “Fear not”. Fear is a thing which is getting quite a problem amongst men. Of course there is a right kind of fear, we need to understand that, a right kind of reverential fear.

The first mention of fear in the scriptures is on account of sin. Adam says, “I heard thy voice in the garden, and I feared, because I am naked”, Genesis 3: 10. That is the cause, the basic cause, of this kind of fear. And of course it is right, if we are in our sins, that we should fear, for God is holy. He has never changed in His holiness and His righteousness—never. But the message in the gospel is that we are not to fear, because a Saviour has been born who is Christ the Lord. A wonderful message this was to these shepherds who were without in the country looking after their flock. They were not in the city; they were persons who could receive communications from heaven. Would that we were more like that! They were persons who were caring for what was of value in the sight of heaven. Would that we were more like that, dear brethren—I fear the influence of the city. Of course this was David’s city, Bethlehem, the royal city of David. And here was the King. His was the royal title to the throne. There was no room for Him in the inn and his cradle was just a manger where the cattle normally fed.

Now we might say, ‘That was force of circumstances. Everybody had come to Bethlehem to be registered who was of that family. It was ordained by the government that they should register in that place and the circumstances were such that there was not enough accommodation.’ But that is not all. The truth is that the manger was appointed by God as the place in which Jesus would lie. This was no mere force of circumstances; this was by deliberate choice; God chose to come this way and to draw so near to men, outside of all their activities, that He might be available to all. Really, the Heir to David’s throne should have had the best place in that inn. He should have had the best rooms reserved. But there was no room—no room! And that is the way, and these are the circumstances, into which Jesus came that He might win our hearts and that He might show us the way that God works, not through the high circles of men, not by anything that would contribute to what men might do, but in lowly grace. He came into circumstances of poverty and smallness. We sang in that hymn of Mr. Darby—
‘O strange yet fit beginning
Of all that life of woe’

I wonder if we are in keeping with that. As I say, I fear the influence and the tendencies of the city, that system that is set up by man to make him self-sufficient. Its danger is that we may be coloured by self-sufficiency, and occupied with all that goes on in the city and thus miss the communications that those who are outside the city receive. We might perhaps look for the best room in the inn, and find that Jesus is not there at all, because the inn would speak to us of the provision that men make for themselves, for their own comfort and satisfaction, and Jesus was outside of it all.

I was impressed by that this morning, a very simple impression but it is very real, that He was here, as Mr. Darby’s hymn which we sang says—‘A houseless, homeless Stranger’. Now that was not just haphazard, because nothing with God is haphazard, but it is to teach us something. The life of Jesus would demonstrate to us our position in the world where He was rejected. He has marked out a path in which, in faith, we are called upon to follow Him. It was outside of all man’s organization—a manger. I can think of nothing more lowly in all that city of Bethlehem than a manger. And there was Jesus. Luke’s presentation is most attractive. Luke is presenting the grace of a Man who draws so near that anyone could approach. You see, if it had been in a palace a man might say—‘Well, I cannot go there’. But a manger—anyone could have gone and found the Saviour there. And this is the way divine grace has taken.

You will notice that it says in verse 9, “the glory of the Lord shone around them” not only was the angel of the Lord there, but there was the divine presence, “the glory of the Lord”, and it shone around them. But the message was, “Fear not”. Oh! there is the Saviour, and He is the answer to fear. If we have a fear as to meeting God on account of what we have done, on account of our sins, the message in the glad tidings is—“Fear not”, because there are glad tidings of great joy. There was a Saviour here born who was to resolve the question of our sins, who was going to die on the cross. His life, as we have sung, commended at every step the grace of God to man in all his need, conveying the grace of God drawing near to men in all their circumstances of pressure and suffering, but, more than that, the cross witnessing to His love. He, voluntarily, took our place to bear the penalty and judgment due to us, that we might go free. So the message is, “Fear not”.

God has provided Himself with a Saviour. Jesus has come into the circumstances and limitations of humanity, and He has come in in such a way, an appointed way of weakness and lowliness, humility, and outward reproach. And having lived that life under the eye of the Father to His perfect satisfaction and delight, He surrendered that life on the cross and bore the judgment that was due to the sinner. He being free of sin Himself (sin having no place in Jesus) He being absolutely holy, took the sinner’s place, and in my place and in your place He bore the full judgment of God against sin, that God “should be just, and justify him that is of the faith of Jesus”, Romans 3: 26. “Fear not”. What a message that is Glad tidings of great joy!

The question that had troubled men through the centuries, through generations, was now to be resolved. And it was resolved on the cross. Men may celebrate His birth, thank God if there is any recognition of the joy that it brought. But everything really depended on His death. Jesus died. That life of sinless perfection was laid down, surrendered. His precious blood flowed from His side, the blood speaking of the life surrendered, the blood without which, Scripture says, there is no remission. That precious blood is the basis on which God can forgive the sinner and justify and bring him into His presence. That work is done. The word is, “Fear not”. Oh think of the feelings of God entering into the glad tidings! We see it in Luke’s gospel on every page; the compassion that moved Jesus, the feelings of His heart towards man. God does not want us to be afraid. Why should we be afraid when Jesus has borne the penalty and has conveyed to us in His every movement here the exceeding grace of God that would draw so near to us, right alongside of us in our need, and would give us the assurance of a work that is completed—give us the assurance of an eternity of joy and blessedness with Him in heaven?

Now I refer to the scripture in Luke 5 because this may become a problem with us. Peter was convicted in the presence of Christ that he was a man full of sin. It might cause fear when we realise the propensities of the flesh. Paul says, “I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, good does not dwell”, Romans 7: 18. We have to come to this in our histories. And Peter is brought to this, he finds and discovers what he is in himself as a wretched, sinful man, able to do nothing good of himself, full of his own wretchedness. We need to come to that, what the flesh is, the total unreliability, the total wretchedness, of the flesh in all its activities. Peter came to it in the presence of the goodness of God, the presence of the power of Jesus, realising who was there. At the word of Jesus they had such a haul of fishes and the net broke. And yet you see what is suggested in this, that whilst Peter was so convicted of his state and the wretchedness of the man that he was, he is held and attracted to Jesus.

Oh that we might prove this, that whilst recognizing the irrecoverable nature of the flesh, of man, the wickedness, the deception that is in the human heart, we might be held consciously and attracted to Jesus. He says, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, Lord.” He felt what he was, but he fell at Jesus’ knees. I believe there would be a suggestion there as to the necessity of the service of Christ as the High Priest for our full emancipation and deliverance—our full salvation. And then the words come from Him, “Fear not”. Oh we might sometimes fear when we realize the weakness and wretchedness of the flesh, but our salvation, dear friends, is in attachment to Jesus. Peter did not go away. He felt his on unsuitability and yet he is held in the power of attraction to that glorious Man, in all the matchless character of His grace as moving amongst men, making healing and blessing available to all.

Peter is held by the attractiveness of Jesus in the consciousness of the need that he has of His service to support him and to sustain him, as he is later in his history when the Lord says, “Behold, Satan has demanded to have you, to sift you as wheat; but I have besought for thee that thy faith fail not”, Luke 22: 31, 32. He stands out as a sample man. Mr. Taylor spoke of him as a sample man and I believe we are all here as a result of the service of Christ in this way, intercessory service, service in the presence of weakness, to hold us to God’s call in grace.

Oh how wonderful it is, that we might be conscious of this in some sense, that we are not to fear, even these circumstances are not to cause us fear, but they are to cause us to be firmly attached to the Saviour who will serve us all the way home—and the Saviour who is living to intercede—the Saviour who is living at this moment in relation to His own. That is to dispel all fear; we can trust in confidence in the power of the One who has begun a work in us, who has died for us, and secured us by His precious blood. That same Person is living to intercede for us that we might be saved completely, “Whence also he is able to save completely those who approach by Him to God, always living to intercede for them”, Hebrews 7: 25. That means saved now, so that in the presence of all the weakness that we may find within, His own work may proceed in power on account of His service on high, and the presence of the Spirit here.

Now I refer briefly to Genesis because here we get another injunction not to fear. “After these things the word of Jehovah came to Abram … Fear not, Abram”. It is when he had renounced any link, in type, with the world, when in the previous chapter he had refused to receive anything from the king of Sodom. It is then that this word comes to Abram, “I am thy shield, thy exceeding great reward”. Oh, dear friends, what God is prepared to be to us as we receive His word! A Saviour indeed, a Saviour from our sins, a living High Priest to save us from ourselves and the activities of the flesh. But then, also, a Saviour in relation to our circumstances here. God says, “I am thy shield”.

A shield is a protection against any attack of the enemy. Think of God saying, ‘Do not be afraid’. The enemy loves to put thoughts of fear, and doubts, into the hearts of God’s people; that is his work. He sometimes says, when we are young, ‘Well, if I am very definite in these circumstances now, I may fail later—I may let the Lord down’. God says, “Fear not, I am thy shield”. We can find a resort in our God. He will protect us from all the efforts of the enemy, from all the power of the enemy. He is our Shield, and He says, “thy exceeding great reward”. Is not that a comfort? Do we know God like that? I think we should know Him more like this as the days go on. Not just what He may do for us, but what He is. He has come so near to us in Jesus that we might know Him. He says, “I am thy shield, thy exceeding great reward”.

After Abraham had made this stand against all the enticements of the world, God was made known to him in this way. Separation from evil, separation from the world, in itself is not an object. It is a necessity, but the objective in view is that we might know God in this way. God is ready to be our reward, as the Spirit of God records in Hebrews, “He is a rewarder of them who seek him out”, Hebrews 11: 6. What a rewarder God is! It is not on the ground of our merit. Oh no! It is on the ground of His matchless grace, on the ground of His sovereign mercy, that He can be a reward to His people, giving compensation and comfort. There is no need to fear—“Fear not”. This element of fear would be dispelled in the knowledge of the God who has come so near to us.

Fear is becoming a problem in the world. There are people going to the doctors day after day, more and more, because of fear. There are special tranquillising drugs, which are in short supply in some parts, because men are getting filled with fear and apprehension. The answer is in God. The word in the glad tidings is, “Fear not, for behold I announce to you glad tidings of great joy”. Peter in chapter 5 of Luke was not to fear, because there was someone, a mighty High Priest, living to support and help, and then the reward, if we are faithful, is in God Himself. I believe, dear friends, that if we follow this, the element of fear will be banished, and we shall find the peace and the joy with which God delights to fill the souls of those who love Him.

Well, may we be encouraged in the fact that fear has been dispelled by the God who has come so near in Jesus, and may our knowledge of Him be increased in the circumstances which He may allow, and which He allows to come upon all men, circumstances of pressure, disappointment, difficulty; they are all, for the christian, calculated to increase our confidence in God and our knowledge of the God who is so near in Jesus. May the word be blessed to us, for His name’s sake.
Thou, Lord, from the heavens wilt come,
Our Deliverer, God’s own Son,
For thy bride, to take her home
To the glory Thou hast won.
Oh, Belov’d, till shadows flee,
Longing hearts wait earnestly.
Thou hast left us, gone on high,
On the Father’s throne to wait;
We, ‘neath dark and stormy sky,
Toil with floods which ne’er abate.
Oh, Belov’d, sustained by Thee,
Longing hearts wait patiently.
Thou art faithful, and Thy love
Ne’er can fail Thy cherished bride.
In Thy Father’s house above,
With Thyself shall we abide.
Oh, Belov’d, thus cheered by Thee,
Longing hearts wait eagerly.
This Thy precious promise, Lord,
“I come quickly”, us inspires.
Sweet as honey is that word,
Telling of Thy heart’s desires.
Oh, Belov’d, we wait for Thee,
Longing hearts Thy face would see.
Lord, to Thee we turn our gaze,
Soon from heaven Thou’lt be revealed;
Then shall beam Thy glorious rays,
Nevermore to be concealed,
Oh, Belov’d, we hail that hour
Of Thy manifested power!
D. Otsing
Translated from the Russian, and slightly adapted. This hymn was found in the papers of the late Mr. Paul Cooper, with a note that it was often sung by the brethren in Russia.
“THE WITNESSES OF JESUS” (Revelation 17: 6)

This choice title is applied to faithful saints in the section of the Revelation dealing with the terrible period of the tribulation. As evil reaches its climax in the great harlot and the beast, there will be martyrs in whom shines a true representation of the precious and holy character of the life of Jesus. God will delight in having the moral continuance of the Man of His pleasure in the darkest day. There could be no greater privilege for us in our responsible lives than to be among those whom heaven can designate as “the witnesses of Jesus”.
‘NATURE ITSELF TEACHES’

Walking through a park recently I was taught two lessons. First, as a downy feather drifted in the breeze, a sparrow snapped it up, and was off to her nest with it. So let us be concerned to gather up spiritual impressions and substance that will help to make our local meetings better furnished spiritually. Then there was a starling rummaging at the bottom of a deep wire refuse basket. So, if we find ourselves in circumstances which are limited and unattractive, let us be alert to find the supplies of comfort and grace that the Lord would surely place for us in that very situation.
